etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Medieval Latin coordinātus, past participle of coordinare (“arrange together”), from Latin co- (“together”) + ordinare (“arrange”), equivalent to co- +‎ ordinate. See ordain and ordinate.

quote.citation: 1745, Edmund Law, Considerations on the State of the World with regard to the Theory of Religion:
quote.text: whether there was one Supreme Governor of the world, or many co-ordinate powers presiding over each country

definitions.definition: (mathematics, cartography, astronomy) A number representing the position of a point along a line, arc, or similar one-dimensional figure.
Something that is equal to another thing.

quote.citation: 1851, John C. Calhoun, A Discourse on the Constitution and Government of the United States‎Wikisource:
quote.text: These are coordinates; because each, in the sphere of its powers, is equal to, and independent of the others; and because the three united make the government.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To place in the same order or rank.

quote.citation: 2017 November 16, Jo Ellison, “Help: the gym has turned us into slobs”, in Financial Times‎[1]:
quote.text: As a fashion editor, I pay obsessive attention to my appearance. Even when I pretend to look insouciant, each look has been painfully considered. The right earrings, coordinating shoes, the careful symmetry of a well-balanced look — these are things that please me. The gym has crushed my sartorial ambitions.
